title: The first question (Berakhot 2a)
hook: the whole Talmud opens by asking from when the evening Shema may be said

segments.voice: Yesterday: the daf, and why every tractate starts on page two. Your line was nobody starts at the true beginning.

How would you open a book people would study for centuries? With God, maybe. With creation, or the meaning of life. The Talmud, the giant library of Jewish law and argument, opens with a question that sounds almost like a text to a friend. From what time can you say the evening Shema? That's the first line. No grand speech, no introduction. Just a practical question about tonight. And it turns out to hold a whole way of seeing time.
screen: `A BOOK FOR THE CENTURIES.` → `HOW DOES IT OPEN?` → `FROM WHAT TIME, TONIGHT?`

segments.voice: The Shema is the line at the heart of Jewish prayer, Hear, O Israel, said morning and evening. The Torah says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." So the rabbis asked: lying down begins when, exactly? The Mishnah answers: from the time the priests go in to eat their holy food, at nightfall. And until when? Three answers. Rabbi Eliezer: until the end of the first watch of the night. The sages: until midnight. Rabban Gamliel: until the first light of dawn. Then a story. Rabban Gamliel's sons came home late from a wedding feast, past midnight. We haven't said the Shema yet, they told him. He said: if dawn hasn't come, you still can, and you still should. Then the Talmud asks a question about the question. Why start with evening, and not morning? One answer: the verse itself says lying down first, then rising up. Another: in the story of creation, evening comes first. "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." That's the order the tradition follows. A Jewish day, Shabbat and every holiday begins in the evening, not at midnight or sunrise. The day starts in the dark and grows toward light. So the Talmud's first question isn't small at all. It asks you to notice the exact moment one day becomes the next, and to meet it with words.
screen: `WHEN THOU LIEST DOWN.` · `THREE ANSWERS: WATCH, MIDNIGHT, DAWN.` · `THE SONS COME HOME LATE.` · `EVENING COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `WHEN DOES EVENING START?`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few days: when does your evening really begin, when you close the laptop, when the kids are asleep, when the light outside changes color, when your phone finally goes face down? Picture meeting that moment on purpose, with one breath or one line you care about. If you pray, it could be the Shema; if not, it could simply be noticing: the day is turning.
Shema, the line at the heart of Jewish prayer. The Talmud's first question asks from when the evening Shema may be said, and answers: from nightfall, because in the Torah the evening comes first.
Your line: when does evening start. Here, the day begins in the dark. That's two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Observant Jews say the Shema in the evening prayer (Maariv) after nightfall and again at bedtime, and every Jewish day, including Shabbat and the holidays, begins at sundown.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the hook called the Talmud 'the most important book of your people', an unsourced superlative a Keeper would dispute (the Torah holds that place); reworded.

Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 is paraphrased: Rabbi Eliezer (until the end of the first watch), the sages (until midnight), Rabban Gamliel (until dawn), and the story of his sons returning from a wedding feast.
The two reasons for starting with evening (the order of Deuteronomy 6:7; the order of Genesis 1:5) both appear on Berakhot 2a; confirm the framing.
The sages' midnight limit is described in the Mishnah as a fence; the script simplifies this. A Keeper may want it mentioned.
Check JPS 1917 wording of Deuteronomy 6:7 and Genesis 1:5.

Review fix: the opening time (from when the priests enter to eat their terumah) is the Mishnah's anonymous first statement, not Rabbi Eliezer's; Rabbi Eliezer gives only the end of the first watch. Script corrected.
The exact moment the day turns (sunset vs. nightfall, bein hashmashot) is itself debated; the teach now says 'begins in the evening' rather than tying the reason to Genesis as settled.
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
